text: Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) play a pivotal role in the delivery of Primary Health Care (PHC) in Nigeria. Discuss five (5) key roles of a CHEW and explain how their functions bridge the gap between the community and the formal health system, in line with the National Standing Orders.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: The Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW) is a multi-skilled health practitioner trained to work in both the community and Primary Health Care (PHC) facilities in Nigeria. Under the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) guidelines and CHPRBN regulatory framework, the CHEW's roles include: 1) Clinical Services: Diagnosing and treating common ailments using the Standing Orders, and administering immunizations. 2) Community Mobilization: Organizing Ward Health Development Committees (WHDCs) and sensitizing community members to participate in health programs. 3) Health Education: Delivering health messages on hygiene, nutrition, maternal and child health, and family planning directly to families. 4) Disease Surveillance: Monitoring and reporting occurrences of notifiable diseases using standard Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) forms. 5) Referral Linkage: Identifying cases beyond their level of competence (e.g., severe dehydration, complicated labor) and referring them promptly to General Hospitals. By spending 50-60% of their time in the community and the remaining time at the facility, CHEWs serve as the primary link between the grassroots population and formal health systems, building trust and ensuring the uptake of essential health services.
markingGuide: 1. Mentions clinical services role and use of National Standing Orders (2 marks)
2. Explains community mobilization role and involvement of WHDC (2 marks)
3. Discusses health education role in community and facility settings (2 marks)
4. Mentions disease surveillance role using IDSR forms (2 marks)
5. Explains referral linkage for complicated cases (2 marks)

text: The Community Health Practitioners Registration Board of Nigeria (CHPRBN) is the regulatory body established to oversee community health practice. Detail the organizational structure of the Board and discuss five (5) of its primary functions in ensuring the standard of community health education and practice in Nigeria.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: The Community Health Practitioners Registration Board of Nigeria (CHPRBN) was established by Decree No. 61 of 1992 (now CAP C19 LFN 2004) as the statutory regulatory authority for all community health practitioners in Nigeria. The Board operates under a governing structure headed by a Chairman appointed by the President, with representation from the Federal Ministry of Health, NPHCDA, state ministries of health, and training institutions, alongside a Registrar who runs the daily administration. The primary functions of the CHPRBN are: 1) Determining the standard of knowledge and skill required to become a registered community health practitioner. 2) Regulating and maintaining registers of qualified Community Health Officers (CHOs), CHEWs, and Junior CHEWs (JCHEWs). 3) Accrediting training institutions, curriculum reviews, and conducting the National Qualifying Examinations. 4) Enforcing professional discipline and ethics through the Investigating Panel and Disciplinary Tribunal. 5) Promoting continuing professional development (CPD) programs to ensure practitioners maintain current clinical knowledge. Through these functions, the CHPRBN maintains high standards, protects public health, and guarantees that practitioners operate safely within their professional scopes of practice.
markingGuide: 1. Identifies the legal establishment of CHPRBN (Decree 61 of 1992 / CAP C19 LFN) (2 marks)
2. Explains the governing structure (Chairman, Registrar, FMOH/NPHCDA reps) (2 marks)
3. Details the function of standard determination and curriculum accreditation (2 marks)
4. Details the function of registration, examinations, and licensing of practitioners (2 marks)
5. Explains disciplinary enforcement (Investigating Panel & Disciplinary Tribunal) and CPD (2 marks)

text: The 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration outlined the fundamental principles of Primary Health Care (PHC). Identify and explain five (5) key principles of PHC and analyze how they are applied within the framework of the Ward Health System and Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) in Nigeria.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: The Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 defined Primary Health Care based on key principles essential for universal health access. 1) Equitable Distribution: Healthcare must be shared equally, prioritizing rural and underserved communities. In Nigeria, this is implemented by building at least one functional PHC per political ward. 2) Community Participation: Active involvement of individuals and families. Nigeria uses the Ward Health Development Committee (WHDC) to engage community leaders in PHC management. 3) Intersectoral Collaboration: Health relies on clean water, sanitation, agriculture, and education. Primary health departments collaborate with ministries of water resources and education. 4) Appropriate Technology: Using affordable, culturally acceptable methods, such as utilizing locally sourced mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) tapes for malnutrition screening. 5) Focus on Prevention: Emphasizing immunizations, health education, and maternal care over curative services. The Ward Health System acts as the operational vehicle for these principles, while the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) provides a financial mechanism (through NHIA and NPHCDA gateways) to guarantee basic services, reducing out-of-pocket spending and ensuring equity for vulnerable populations.
markingGuide: 1. Identifies and defines Equitable Distribution and its Nigerian application (functional PHC per ward) (2 marks)
2. Explains Community Participation and the role of the WHDC (2 marks)
3. Outlines Intersectoral Collaboration with examples (water, education) (2 marks)
4. Explains Appropriate Technology and preventive focus with examples (2 marks)
5. Connects the principles to the Ward Health System and BHCPF funding mechanisms (2 marks)

text: Communication is an essential clinical and community tool for a Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW). Describe the six steps of the GATHER acronym used in counseling and explain how a CHEW can apply this framework to counsel a first-time mother on exclusive breastfeeding.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: The GATHER framework is a systematic, client-centered approach to counseling. For a first-time mother on exclusive breastfeeding, the CHEW applies the steps as follows: 1) G - Greet the client: Greet the mother warmly and respectfully in the local language, establishing rapport. 2) A - Ask the client: Ask about her understanding of breastfeeding, her plans, and any concerns or cultural beliefs. 3) T - Tell the client: Provide clear information on exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, explaining benefits like immunity and nutrition, while dispelling myths. 4) H - Help the client: Assist the mother to make an informed decision, addressing barriers such as returning to work, and demonstrating correct positioning and attachment. 5) E - Explain what to do: Explain practical aspects, such as feeding on demand (8-12 times daily) and signs of good attachment (chin touching breast, wide mouth, slow deep sucks). 6) R - Return for follow-up: Arrange the next appointment, usually matching her immunization schedule (6 weeks), and advise her to return immediately if breast engorgement or fever occurs. This structured counseling ensures the mother feels supported, informed, and capable of practicing exclusive breastfeeding.
markingGuide: 1. Defines 'G' (Greet) and 'A' (Ask) with client-specific breastfeeding examples (2 marks)
2. Defines 'T' (Tell) with correct explanation of exclusive breastfeeding (2 marks)
3. Defines 'H' (Help) with problem-solving and support techniques (2 marks)
4. Defines 'E' (Explain) detailing practical feeding instructions (frequency, positioning) (2 marks)
5. Defines 'R' (Return) detailing follow-up arrangements and warning signs (2 marks)

text: A Community Health Diagnosis (Community Assessment) is a prerequisite for effective community intervention. Outline and explain the seven (7) major steps involved in conducting a community health diagnosis, from planning to feedback delivery.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: A Community Health Diagnosis is a systematic process of identifying health needs, resources, and priorities of a community. The steps include: 1) Preliminary Contact and Sensitization: Meeting community leaders and the Ward Health Development Committee (WHDC) to explain the purpose and obtain entry permission. 2) Planning and Tool Development: Defining objectives, choosing data collection methods (questionnaires, focus groups, mapping), and training the assessment team. 3) Data Collection: Administering tools to collect quantitative data (e.g., immunization rates, water sources) and qualitative data (community perceptions of health problems). 4) Data Collation and Analysis: Sorting, coding, and analyzing the collected data to identify common diseases, risk factors, and available resources. 5) Priority Setting: Using criteria like magnitude, severity, and feasibility of solution to rank identified problems (often using a prioritization matrix with community input). 6) Drawing up the Action plan: Designing an intervention detailing who, what, when, and how, including resource mobilization. 7) Presentation of Findings/Feedback: Presenting the results to the community in a town hall meeting, ensuring they take ownership of the findings and participate in implementing the solutions.
markingGuide: 1. Explains Community Entry/Sensitization (WHDC involvement) (1.5 marks)
2. Describes Planning and Tool Development phase (1.5 marks)
3. Details Data Collection methods (quantitative/qualitative) (1.5 marks)
4. Explains Data Collation and Analysis process (1.5 marks)
5. Discusses Priority Setting criteria (1.5 marks)
6. Outlines drafting the Action Plan (1.5 marks)
7. Discusses feedback delivery to the community (town hall) (1 mark)

text: Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) in Primary Health Care facilities is critical for patient and healthcare worker safety. Discuss standard precautions in IPC, detailing the procedure for hand hygiene and the color-coded waste management system used in Nigerian PHCs.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Standard precautions in Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) are basic infection prevention practices that apply to all patient care, regardless of suspected or confirmed status. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure, requiring washing with soap and running water (using the 11-step WHO technique) or using an alcohol-based hand rub before and after patient contact, after exposure to body fluids, and after touching patient surroundings. In Nigerian PHC facilities, healthcare waste must be segregated at the point of generation using the national color-coded system: 1) Black bags/bins: Non-hazardous, general administrative waste (paper, food peels). 2) Yellow bags/bins: Infectious clinical waste (used dressings, gloves, blood-soaked cotton). 3) Red bags/bins: Highly infectious waste (sputum cups from TB patients, viral hemorrhagic fever materials). 4) Yellow safety boxes: Sharps waste (needles, syringes, ampoules, lancets). Sharps boxes must be filled only up to the 3/4 mark to prevent needle-stick injuries. Proper adherence to these protocols prevents nosocomial infections and protects the surrounding community.
markingGuide: 1. Defines standard precautions and states hand hygiene importance (2 marks)
2. Outlines WHO handwashing technique/occasions (5 moments) (2 marks)
3. Explains Black and Yellow bag waste classification (2 marks)
4. Explains Red bag waste classification (2 marks)
5. Explains Yellow Safety Box use for sharps (filling limit, examples) (2 marks)

text: Primary Health Care delivery is multi-disciplinary and depends on effective teamwork. Identify the core members of a standard PHC facility team in Nigeria and explain the role of each member in achieving health targets.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: A standard Primary Health Care facility in Nigeria operates on a multidisciplinary team model, where each member contributes specialized skills to provide comprehensive, integrated care. The core team members include: 1) Facility Manager (often a CHO or Senior CHEW): Coordinates overall clinical and administrative activities, supervises staff, manages resources, and liaises with the Local Government Area (LGA) health department. 2) Community Health Extension Worker (CHEW): Conducts clinical consultations for minor ailments, administers vaccines, manages records, and spends a significant portion of time in the community conducting home visits. 3) Junior CHEW (JCHEW): Conducts home visits, performs basic first aid, assists in community mobilization, and refers cases to the CHEW. 4) Nurse/Midwife: Manages antenatal care, conducts normal deliveries, provides post-natal care, and leads family planning services. 5) Environmental Health Officer/Technician: Monitors sanitation, inspects local food vendors, and oversees solid and liquid waste management within the facility and community. 6) Community Health Recorder/Clerk: Manages the Health Management Information System (HMIS) registers, compiling daily patient visits and reporting monthly data. Effective collaboration among these roles ensures seamless patient care, high immunization coverage, and robust community outreach.
markingGuide: 1. Defines the concept of a multidisciplinary team in PHC (1 mark)
2. Outlines the role of the Facility Manager (CHO/Senior CHEW) (2 marks)
3. Details the complementary roles of CHEWs and JCHEWs (3 marks)
4. Details the role of the Nurse/Midwife in maternal/child health (2 marks)
5. Discusses the roles of the Environmental Health officer and Health Recorder (2 marks)

text: Nigeria transitioned from the traditional antenatal care model to Focused Antenatal Care (FANC). Outline the schedule of visits under the 2016 WHO/FMOH FANC guidelines (minimum of 8 contacts) and discuss the essential packages of care delivered during these contacts.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Focused Antenatal Care (FANC) emphasizes quality of care over quantity of visits. The current WHO and Federal Ministry of Health (FMOH) guidelines recommend a minimum of 8 antenatal contacts: Contact 1: Under 12 weeks of pregnancy; Contact 2: 20 weeks; Contact 3: 26 weeks; Contact 4: 30 weeks; Contact 5: 34 weeks; Contact 6: 36 weeks; Contact 7: 38 weeks; and Contact 8: 40 weeks. The essential packages of care delivered during these visits comprise: 1) Early Detection and Management: Routine monitoring of blood pressure, urinalysis (for proteinuria), symphysio-fundal height, and fetal heart rate. 2) Prevention of Diseases: Administering Tetanus Toxoid (TD) vaccination, Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (SP) for Intermittent Preventive Treatment of malaria (IPTp) starting from 16 weeks (at least 3 doses, 1 month apart), and iron/folic acid supplementation. 3) Health Promotion and Education: Counselling on nutrition, birth preparedness (saving money, choosing a skilled birth attendant, identifying transport), and exclusive breastfeeding. 4) Screening and Treatment: Testing for HIV (PMTCT), Syphilis, Hepatitis B, and anemia, with immediate therapy or referral if positive. This comprehensive approach reduces maternal morbidity and neonatal mortality.
markingGuide: 1. Lists the 8 contact schedule with correct gestational ages (3 marks)
2. Explains routine monitoring and screening tests (BP, urine, HIV, anemia) (2.5 marks)
3. Details preventative interventions (TD vaccine, SP for IPTp, Iron/Folate) (2.5 marks)
4. Discusses health promotion and birth preparedness counselling (2 marks)

text: The Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) in Nigeria protects children from vaccine-preventable diseases. Detail the current national EPI immunization schedule from birth to 15 months, specifying the antigens, routes, and doses. Explain the cold chain requirements for vaccine storage at the PHC level.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Nigeria's EPI schedule targets children under one year to prevent childhood illnesses. The schedule is: At Birth: BCG (0.05ml ID), Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV0 - 2 drops oral), Hepatitis B0 (0.5ml IM). At 6 Weeks: Penta1 (DPT-HepB-Hib - 0.5ml IM), OPV1 (2 drops), Rotavirus 1 (0.5ml oral), Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV1 - 0.5ml IM), Fractional IPV1 (0.1ml ID). At 10 Weeks: Penta2, OPV2, Rota2, PCV2. At 14 Weeks: Penta3, OPV3, PCV3, Fractional IPV2 (0.1ml ID). At 9 Months: Measles 1 (0.5ml SC), Yellow Fever (0.5ml SC), Meningitis A (0.5ml SC). At 15 Months: Measles 2 (0.5ml SC). At the PHC level, the Cold Chain is preserved using Solar Direct Drive (SDD) refrigerators, maintaining temperatures between +2°C and +8°C. Vaccines must be organized correctly: OPV, Measles, and Yellow Fever are heat-sensitive and placed in the coldest parts, while freeze-sensitive vaccines (Penta, PCV, Hepatitis B, TD) must never touch the freezer plate or ice packs. Freeze indicators (like FreezeTag) and twice-daily temperature logs are mandatory. During outreach, vaccines are transported in vaccine carriers containing four conditioned ice packs, keeping them viable for up to 48 hours.
markingGuide: 1. Accurately details EPI schedule at Birth and 6 weeks (antigens, routes, doses) (2.5 marks)
2. Details EPI schedule at 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 9 months, and 15 months (2.5 marks)
3. Explains the +2°C to +8°C temperature range and SDD refrigerators (2 marks)
4. Explains the segregation of heat-sensitive and freeze-sensitive vaccines (2 marks)
5. Outlines vaccine carrier and outreach temperature maintenance (1 mark)

text: Malnutrition remains a major public health challenge in Nigeria. Detail the clinical assessment of an under-5 child for malnutrition. Explain the classification of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) versus Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM), and outline the Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP) management protocol using Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF).
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Assessment of malnutrition involves anthropometric, clinical, and dietary evaluations. Anthropometry includes measuring weight-for-height/length, checking for bilateral pitting pedal edema, and measuring the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) using a standard tape. Classification is as follows: 1) Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM): Defined by MUAC < 11.5 cm, weight-for-height Z-score < -3, or the presence of bilateral pitting pedal edema (kwashiorkor). 2) Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM): Defined by MUAC between 11.5 cm and 12.5 cm, and weight-for-height Z-score between -2 and -3, without edema. For SAM children without medical complications (poor appetite, severe vomiting, high fever, severe anemia, or severe edema), management is done at the Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP): 1) Appetite Test: The child must pass the appetite test by consuming a prescribed portion of RUTF under observation. 2) RUTF Prescription: Calculated based on weight (approx. 200 kcal/kg/day). 3) Routine Medications: Administered on day 1 (Amoxicillin for 7 days, single-dose deworming with Albendazole/Mebendazole if > 1 year, Vitamin A if not received in past month, and Malaria screening/treatment). 4) Follow-up: Weekly visits to monitor weight, MUAC, and supply RUTF. Severe cases with complications are referred to an Inpatient Stabilization Centre (SC) for F-75/F-100 therapeutic milk treatment.
markingGuide: 1. Describes anthropometric assessment methods (MUAC, Weight-for-Height, Edema) (2.5 marks)
2. Distinguishes MAM and SAM using exact cut-offs (MUAC and Z-scores) (2.5 marks)
3. Explains the role and execution of the RUTF Appetite Test (1.5 marks)
4. Details OTP routine medications (Amoxicillin, Albendazole, Vit A, Antimalarials) (2 marks)
5. Outlines weekly follow-up and inpatient referral criteria (1.5 marks)

text: A 28-year-old mother of three (last child aged 6 months) visits your PHC facility wishing to space her next pregnancy. Apply the GATHER approach step-by-step to counsel her, detailing how you would help her choose and initiate a suitable family planning method.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Applying the GATHER counseling framework for this client: 1) G - Greet: Greet the mother warmly, introduce yourself, and ensure privacy. Praise her for deciding to space her children. 2) A - Ask: Ask about her reproductive history, breastfeeding status, menstrual cycle, medical history, and if she has a preferred method. (Since her last child is 6 months, ask if she is still exclusively breastfeeding or has started complementary feeding). 3) T - Tell: Tell her about the available methods compatible with her status, such as Progestogen-only Pills (POPs), Implants (Implanon/Jadelle), Injectables (DMPA/Sayana Press), or Copper IUDs. Explain their mechanism, effectiveness, and common side effects (e.g., changes in bleeding patterns). 4) H - Help: Help her choose. She expresses a preference for a long-acting method that won't interfere with breastfeeding. Guide her to choose Implants (effective for 3-5 years) or IUD (effective for 10 years). She selects the subdermal implant. 5) E - Explain: Explain how the implant is inserted under local anesthesia in the inner upper arm, how it works, and common side effects like minor spotting. Tell her it does not protect against STIs/HIV, so condom use is encouraged. 6) R - Return: Schedule a follow-up visit in 1 week to check the insertion site, and then as needed. Instruct her to return immediately if she experiences severe headache, local infection at the insertion site, or if the implant feels dislodged. This structured counseling empowers the client and supports compliance.
markingGuide: 1. Demonstrates Greeting and Asking relative to the client's postpartum/breastfeeding status (2 marks)
2. Details the 'Tell' step, listing options compatible with lactation (2 marks)
3. Details the 'Help' step, guiding the client through selecting a method based on her preference (2 marks)
4. Explains the insertion procedure, mechanism, and side effects of the chosen method (2 marks)
5. Details the 'Return' step, specifying warning signs and follow-up timeline (2 marks)

text: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) is a core strategy in reducing HIV incidence in children. Describe the four (4) prongs of the PMTCT strategy and outline the clinical protocol for managing an HIV-positive pregnant woman and her exposed infant at a PHC facility.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: The comprehensive PMTCT strategy consists of four prongs: Prong 1: Primary prevention of HIV infection among women of childbearing age. Prong 2: Prevention of unintended pregnancies among HIV-positive women. Prong 3: Prevention of HIV transmission from HIV-positive women to their infants. Prong 4: Provision of treatment, care, and support to HIV-positive mothers, their infants, and families. For an HIV-positive pregnant woman identified at a PHC facility: 1) Antiretroviral Therapy (ART): Initiate Triple ART immediately (typically Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir - TLD) regardless of CD4 count or gestational age, and maintain for life. 2) Safe Delivery: Promote skilled birth delivery, avoiding artificial rupture of membranes and routine episiotomy to minimize blood exposure. 3) Infant Prophylaxis: Administer Nevirapine (NVP) syrup daily to the infant from birth to 6 weeks. If the mother was not on ART before delivery, combine NVP with Zidovudine (AZT) for 6 weeks. 4) Infant Feeding: Counsel on exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, followed by complementary feeding up to 12 months, provided the mother is virally suppressed on ART. Mixed feeding must be avoided as it damages the gut mucosa, increasing HIV transmission risk. 5) Early Infant Diagnosis (EID): Collect Dry Blood Spot (DBS) for DNA PCR testing at 6 weeks of age.
markingGuide: 1. Correctly lists and explains the 4 prongs of the PMTCT strategy (2.5 marks)
2. Outlines immediate TLD initiation and safe delivery practices for the mother (2.5 marks)
3. Details infant ARV prophylaxis regimen and duration (2 marks)
4. Explains safe infant feeding practices (exclusive breastfeeding vs. mixed feeding risk) (2 marks)
5. Mentions DNA PCR testing at 6 weeks for Early Infant Diagnosis (EID) (1 mark)

text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic with acute watery diarrhoea. Describe the clinical signs used to classify the hydration status of the child according to IMCI guidelines, and outline the management protocols under Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Assessment and classification of dehydration in a child with acute watery diarrhoea are based on IMCI guidelines, categorizing the child into three groups: 1) No Dehydration: General condition is alert; eyes are normal; tears are present; mouth/tongue are wet; skin pinch goes back immediately. Plan A (Home management) is initiated: give extra fluids (ORS, coconut water, or gruels), continue breastfeeding, give Zinc tablets (20 mg daily for 10-14 days; 10 mg if <6 months), feed the child, and teach the mother warning signs to return immediately. 2) Some Dehydration: Child is restless/irritable; eyes are sunken; thirsty (drinks eagerly); skin pinch goes back slowly. Plan B (Clinic rehydration) is initiated: give a specified volume of ORS (approx. 75 ml/kg) over 4 hours. Monitor progress. If rehydrated, transition to Plan A. Give Zinc. 3) Severe Dehydration: Child is lethargic or unconscious; eyes are sunken; not able to drink or drinks poorly; skin pinch goes back very slowly (>2 seconds). Plan C (Urgent rehydration) is initiated: Start IV fluids immediately (Ringer's Lactate or Normal Saline - 100 ml/kg split into 30 ml/kg and 70 ml/kg over specific hours based on age). If IV is not possible, insert a nasogastric tube or refer urgently. Give Zinc once the child can swallow.
markingGuide: 1. Classifies No Dehydration and details Plan A (Zinc, home fluids, warning signs) (3 marks)
2. Classifies Some Dehydration and details Plan B (ORS calculation and timeline) (3 marks)
3. Classifies Severe Dehydration and details Plan C (IV fluids, alternatives) (3 marks)
4. Identifies the correct dosage of Zinc for under-5s (1 mark)

text: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks gestation is rushed to your PHC facility. Discuss five (5) obstetric danger signs in pregnancy and outline the immediate stabilization and referral steps you must take as a CHEW.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Obstetric danger signs are life-threatening conditions during pregnancy that require urgent intervention. The five key danger signs include: 1) Vaginal Bleeding: Suggestive of placenta praevia or abruptio placentae. 2) Convulsions/Fits: Indicative of eclampsia. 3) Severe Headache with Blurred Vision: Indicative of severe pre-eclampsia. 4) Severe Abdominal Pain: Can suggest uterine rupture or ectopic pregnancy. 5) High Fever with Vaginal Discharge: Indicative of systemic infection or chorioamnionitis. As a CHEW, immediate stabilization and referral protocol involves: 1) Rapid Assessment: Check airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs (BP, pulse, temperature). 2) Establish IV Access: Secure a wide-bore cannula (16G or 18G) and start normal saline or Ringer's lactate. If pre-eclampsia/eclampsia is suspected, administer Magnesium Sulfate (MgSO4) following the national dosage protocol (loading dose: 4g IV slowly and 10g IM, 5g in each buttock) after checking respiratory rate and patellar reflexes. 3) Position the Patient: Place the woman in the left lateral position to optimize uterine perfusion and prevent supine hypotension. 4) Document and Communicate: Complete a detailed referral note detailing vital signs, administered treatments (especially MgSO4 or IV fluids), and reason for referral. 5) Accompanied Referral: Arrange transport and accompany the patient to the nearest CEmONC facility, maintaining resuscitation measures en route.
markingGuide: 1. Identifies five (5) obstetric danger signs and their clinical implications (2.5 marks)
2. Explains initial assessment and establishing IV access (2 marks)
3. Details administration of Magnesium Sulfate for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, with safety checks (2.5 marks)
4. Outlines patient positioning (left lateral) and writing the referral note (2 marks)
5. Emphasizes the need to accompany the patient to the CEmONC facility (1 mark)

text: Outbreak investigation is critical to controlling infectious diseases. Outline and explain the ten (10) systematic steps of conducting a localized disease outbreak investigation in a community.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: An outbreak investigation is a systematic epidemiological process conducted to identify the source, control the spread, and prevent future occurrences of a disease. The 10 standard steps are: 1) Prepare for Fieldwork: Gather equipment, personal protective equipment (PPE), data collection tools, and secure administrative clearances. 2) Establish the Existence of an Outbreak: Compare the current number of cases with baseline data to confirm an excess. 3) Verify the Diagnosis: Confirm clinical signs and review laboratory findings to ensure accurate identification of the pathogen. 4) Construct a Working Case Definition: Establish criteria (person, place, time, clinical symptoms) to identify cases. 5) Find Cases Systematically and Record Information: Active case searching in clinics and communities, listing cases on a line list. 6) Perform Descriptive Epidemiology: Analyze data by time (epidemic curve), place (spot map), and person (age, sex, occupation). 7) Develop Hypotheses: Propose the likely source, vehicle of transmission, and risk factors based on descriptive data. 8) Evaluate Hypotheses Analytically: Compare risk factors among cases and healthy controls (e.g., case-control or cohort studies). 9) Implement Control and Prevention Measures: Immediate interventions (e.g., chlorinating wells, isolating patients, distributing bed nets) tailored to the source. 10) Communicate Findings: Share reports with local authorities, FMOH, and the community to improve future surveillance.
markingGuide: 1. Explains preparation, establishing outbreak existence, and verifying diagnosis (3 marks)
2. Discusses creating a case definition and active case finding (2 marks)
3. Explains descriptive epidemiology (time, place, person) and hypothesis development (2 marks)
4. Outlines hypothesis evaluation, control/prevention measures, and reporting findings (3 marks)

text: The Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system is Nigeria’s framework for monitoring infectious diseases. Identify the target diseases under the IDSR system, classify them, and describe the reporting channels and timelines from the PHC facility to the federal level.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) integrates clinical and laboratory data to trigger public health action. Diseases under IDSR are categorized into: 1) Epidemic-Prone Diseases: Cholera, Lassa Fever, Yellow Fever, Measles, CSF (Meningitis), Monkeypox, Covid-19. 2) Diseases Targeted for Eradication/Elimination: Neonatal Tetanus, Poliomyelitis (AFP), Guinea Worm, Lymphatic Filariasis. 3) Diseases of Public Health Importance: Tuberculosis, Malaria, HIV/AIDS, Malnutrition, Maternal Deaths. The reporting channels and timelines are: 1) Immediate Reporting (within 24 hours): For epidemic-prone diseases or single cases of eradication-target diseases (e.g., AFP, Lassa). The CHEW contacts the LGA DSNO immediately via phone or SMS, followed by filling the IDSR 001A form. 2) Weekly Reporting (by Monday noon): Utilizing the IDSR 002 form to report aggregated weekly numbers of epidemic-prone diseases to the DSNO. 3) Monthly Reporting (by the 5th of the following month): Utilizing the IDSR 003 form for routine diseases of public health importance. The DSNO compiles reports from all PHCs and submits them to the State DSNO, who in turn validates and uploads the data to the NCDC and Federal Ministry of Health (FMOH) database (using platforms like SORMAS or DHIS2). This structured reporting enables early detection of outbreaks and timely national response.
markingGuide: 1. Classifies IDSR diseases into Epidemic-prone, Eradication targets, and Public Health importance (3 marks)
2. Outlines immediate reporting timelines (within 24 hours) and tools (IDSR 001A) (2 marks)
3. Details weekly reporting timelines (Monday noon) and tools (IDSR 002) (2 marks)
4. Details monthly reporting timelines (by 5th) and tools (IDSR 003) (2 marks)
5. Explains the upward flow of data from PHC -> LGA DSNO -> State DSNO -> NCDC/FMOH (1 mark)

text: Access to safe water is a major determinant of community health. Identify the main sources of water in rural communities and describe four (4) household-level water treatment methods that a CHEW should teach community members.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: In rural Nigerian communities, common water sources include surface water (rivers, streams, ponds), shallow hand-dug wells, boreholes, and rainwater harvesting. Surface water and shallow wells are highly susceptible to contamination from agricultural runoff, animal waste, and open defecation, leading to waterborne diseases like cholera, typhoid, and dysentery. To ensure safety at the point of use, the CHEW must educate families on the following household-level water treatment methods: 1) Boiling: The simplest and most effective method. Water should be brought to a rolling boil for at least 1 to 3 minutes to kill pathogenic bacteria, viruses, and parasites. 2) Chemical Disinfection (Chlorination): Using liquid bleach or chlorine tablets (e.g., WaterGuard, Aquatabs). Add the correct dosage, stir, and let it stand for 30 minutes before drinking. 3) Filtration: Using local sand/gravel filters, ceramic pot filters, or Biosand filters to remove suspended solids, debris, and larger pathogens. For muddy water, this must precede disinfection. 4) Solar Disinfection (SODIS): Filling clean, clear PET plastic bottles with water and exposing them to direct sunlight for at least 6 hours (or 2 days if cloudy). The UV radiation and heat kill pathogens. Proper storage in narrow-necked, covered containers with a tap or dedicated ladle prevents recontamination.
markingGuide: 1. Identifies common rural water sources and explains their vulnerability to contamination (2 marks)

text: You are required to organize a health education campaign on Lassa fever prevention in a community with a recent outbreak. Outlines the steps you would take to plan, implement, and evaluate this campaign.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Planning and implementing a health education campaign requires a structured approach to achieve behavioral change. The steps are: 1) Planning Phase: - Assessment: Analyze the community's knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding Lassa fever (e.g., grain storage, bush burning). - Define Objectives: Formulate SMART objectives (e.g., 'Increase the percentage of households storing food in covered metal containers from 30% to 80% within 3 months'). - Target Audience: Focus on food handlers, farmers, and mothers. - Resource Mobilization: Secure budget, posters, megaphones, and enlist local volunteers. 2) Implementation Phase: - Community Entry: Visit the traditional ruler and the Ward Health Development Committee (WHDC) to gain support. - Channel Selection: Use multiple channels (town announcers, radio jingles in local dialects, health talks at clinics, drama groups). - Message Dissemination: Focus on actionable messages: 'Keep food covered', 'Block rat holes', 'Do not touch body fluids of sick people', 'Clean surroundings'. Keep rats away from homes. 3) Evaluation Phase: - Process Evaluation: Measure inputs and activities (number of posters distributed, meetings held, people reached). - Outcome/Impact Evaluation: Conduct post-campaign surveys or home visits to verify behavior change (e.g., reduction in bush burning, cleaner yards, and early reporting of fever cases to the PHC). Evaluation ensures lessons are learned for future campaigns.
markingGuide: 1. Outlines the Planning Phase, including community assessment and SMART objectives (3.5 marks)
2. Explains the Implementation Phase, focusing on community entry, channels, and specific messages (3.5 marks)
3. Details the Evaluation Phase, distinguishing between process and outcome evaluation (3 marks)

text: A rural community in your LGA has consistently recorded low immunisation coverage. Discuss five (5) community mobilisation strategies you would implement to engage the community and improve immunization uptake.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Improving immunization coverage in a resistant or underserved community requires active community engagement rather than top-down clinical instructions. The following five community mobilization strategies are highly effective: 1) Engagement of Traditional and Religious Leaders: Meet with local chiefs, imams, and pastors. Because they hold high authority, securing their public endorsement of vaccines helps dispel rumors and build trust. 2) Reactivation and Empowerment of the Ward Health Development Committee (WHDC): Train WHDC members to monitor facility performance, identify defaulters, and organize transport for remote families during immunization days. 3) Utilizing Voluntary Community Health Workers (VCHWs) or Town Announcers: Equip local volunteers and town announcers with megaphones to announce immunization clinics, trace defaulted children, and conduct house-to-house sensitization. 4) Organizing Integrated Outreach Services ('Mop-up' Campaigns): Instead of waiting at the facility, set up temporary immunization posts at local markets, community squares, or schools during peak hours. Pair vaccines with free services like vitamin A distribution, worm treatment, and maternal health checks to attract families. 5) Enlisting Women Groups and Market Associations: Partner with local women's cooperatives, trade groups, and mother-to-mother support groups. Empowering mothers to educate their peers utilizes social networks to promote vaccination as a collective responsibility.
markingGuide: 1. Details mobilization of traditional and religious leaders to address vaccine hesitancy (2 marks)
2. Explains WHDC engagement and default tracing (2 marks)
3. Outlines the role of VCHWs and local town announcers (2 marks)
4. Discusses integrated outreach services and pairing of health interventions (2 marks)
5. Explains partnering with women's groups and peer-to-peer networks (2 marks)

text: Malaria is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Nigeria. Describe the comprehensive measures for malaria prevention and control at the community and household levels, and explain the role of the CHEW in implementing these measures.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: Malaria control in Nigeria is guided by the National Malaria Elimination Programme (NMEP) and focuses on vector control, prevention during pregnancy, and prompt case management. At the community and household level, prevention strategies include: 1) Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs): Consistent use of LLINs every night by all family members, especially under-5 children and pregnant women. Nets must be hung in shade to air for 24 hours before use and washed gently. 2) Environmental Sanitation: Eliminating breeding sites for Anopheles mosquitoes by draining stagnant water, filling potholes, clearing overgrown weeds around houses, and proper refuse disposal. 3) Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp): Ensuring pregnant women receive Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (SP) under Direct Observed Therapy (DOT) at the facility starting at 16 weeks gestation. The role of the CHEW in these efforts includes: - Distribution: Participating in mass LLIN distribution campaigns and routine net distribution during antenatal clinics. - Health Education: Educating community members on correct LLIN usage, malaria transmission, and debunking myths. - Diagnostic and Treatment Services: Performing Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDT) for all fever cases at the facility and community level, and administering Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) like Artemether-Lumefantrine for confirmed simple malaria, while referring severe cases immediately.
markingGuide: 1. Details LLIN usage and care instructions at the household level (2.5 marks)
2. Explains environmental sanitation/source reduction methods (2 marks)
3. Details IPTp administration for pregnant women (2 marks)
4. Explains the CHEW's role in health education and net distribution (1.5 marks)
5. Outlines the CHEW's clinical role in malaria diagnosis (RDT) and treatment (ACT) (2 marks)

text: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as hypertension and diabetes are rising in Nigeria. Discuss the role of the CHEW in the prevention, early detection, and lifestyle management of NCDs at the Primary Health Care level.
explanation: MODEL ANSWER: The rising burden of NCDs in Nigeria necessitates proactive community-level action. The CHEW's role is categorized into three key areas: 1) Prevention through Health Promotion: Educating the community on NCD risk factors. The CHEW encourages lifestyle modifications such as reducing salt and sugar intake, avoiding processed foods, increasing physical activity, stopping tobacco use, and limiting alcohol consumption. They promote traditional diets rich in vegetables and whole grains. 2) Screening and Early Detection: Conducting routine screenings during clinic visits and community outreach. This includes measuring blood pressure for all adults (using correct technique to identify hypertension), checking blood glucose levels using glucometers, and calculating Body Mass Index (BMI) using weight and height measurements. 3) Lifestyle Management and Follow-Up: Counseling diagnosed patients on medication adherence, monitoring for complications, and supporting dietary compliance. The CHEW organizes support groups and schedules regular follow-up visits to check BP and glucose. They play a critical role in referring patients with uncontrolled blood pressure (>140/90 mmHg despite lifestyle changes or >160/100 mmHg initially) or high blood sugar to medical officers, thereby reducing complications like stroke, kidney failure, and diabetic coma.
markingGuide: 1. Details prevention strategies focusing on lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol) (3 marks)
2. Explains screening methods (blood pressure, blood glucose, BMI measurement) (3 marks)
3. Outlines the CHEW's role in medication adherence and follow-up (2 marks)
4. Explains referral criteria for uncontrolled or severe NCD cases (2 marks)
